title: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)
word: The mustard seed and the yeast
hook: the kingdom starts smaller than you'd notice and works through everything

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sower, and our first parable: seed on the path, the rocks, the thorns, the good ground. Your line was be good ground. What kind of ground were you? Day forty-four. Two more seeds today, very small ones.

Hold a mustard seed on your fingertip and you'll barely see it. It's about the size of a pinhead. Drop it on the kitchen floor and you'll never find it again. Now think of a small lump of yeast, a spoonful of old dough from yesterday's bread. You wouldn't look at either one twice. And that's exactly what Jesus reaches for when people ask what the kingdom of heaven is like. Not a palace. Not an army. Not a thunderclap. A seed you could lose, and a bit of dough a woman hides in the flour. Today: two of the shortest parables he told, three verses between them.
screen: `A SEED THE SIZE OF A PINHEAD.` → `A SPOONFUL OF OLD DOUGH.` → `THIS IS WHAT THE KINGDOM IS LIKE?`

segments.voice: The first, in the Douay-Rheims: "The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field." The least of all the seeds, Jesus says, but when it's grown it becomes a tree, and the birds of the air come and live in its branches. The mustard of Galilee grows fast into a big, sprawling shrub, taller than a person. Some scholars point out it's also a bit of a weed: once it's in your field, it spreads. The kingdom isn't neat. It takes over. Then the second parable, just one sentence long: "The kingdom of heaven is like to leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened." Leaven is yeast, but not the packet kind. It was a lump of old, sour dough kept back from the last batch. And look at the verb: she hid it. You can't see it working. And three measures of flour is huge, very roughly fifty or sixty pounds, bread for a whole village. One small hidden lump, and the whole mass rises. Two pictures, one idea. God's work in the world starts too small to notice, works out of sight, and goes all the way through. Catholics love a saint who lived this. Thérèse of Lisieux, a young Carmelite nun who died at twenty-four, called her path the little way: doing ordinary, tiny things with great love. The Church later named her a Doctor of the Church, one of the few women given that title.
screen: `THE LEAST OF ALL SEEDS.` · `A SHRUB THAT SPREADS.` · `LEAVEN, HIDDEN IN THE FLOUR.` · `THÉRÈSE'S LITTLE WAY.` · then, large: `UNTIL THE WHOLE WAS LEAVENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one tiny good thing. Settle and breathe. Let your day come to mind, hour by hour. Somewhere in it is a place for something very small: a kind word to the person at the register, a text that says thinking of you, a cup put away that isn't yours. Not a project. A seed. Pick one. See yourself doing it. It won't look like much. It isn't supposed to. If you pray, you can offer it to God in advance. The bell holds the time.
The mustard seed and the yeast. Two parables of small, hidden things that grow through everything. Today's word.
screen: `THE MUSTARD SEED AND THE YEAST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: small is how it starts. Today, do the one tiny good thing, and don't wait to see what it grows into. Day forty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics hear these parables at Sunday Mass in summer, and many take up Saint Thérèse of Lisieux's little way, doing small daily tasks with great love as a path of holiness.

fork.setup: someone asks you to describe the kingdom of heaven in one picture. what does Jesus choose?
options: a great king on a throne.
a seed so small you could lose it.
a mighty army on the march.
fork.reveal: a mustard seed, and then a lump of leaven hidden in flour. small, hidden, and working all the way through.

original.note: Greek: leaven, a lump of fermented dough kept back to start the next batch.

trapdoor: what you thought: small things can become big things.
what it means: God's work starts too small to notice, works hidden, and spreads through everything.
what a scholar hears: mustard spreads like a weed, and the woman hides the leaven in about fifty pounds of flour: bread for a village.

sources.ref: Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 13:31 and 13:33 given from memory; confirm.
Three measures (sata) of flour: estimates run from about 40 to 60 pounds; the script says 'very roughly fifty or sixty pounds'. Confirm.
Mustard as a spreading, weedy plant (Pliny the Elder notes this): a scholarly observation; confirm phrasing.
Thérèse of Lisieux (1873–1897), died aged 24; declared Doctor of the Church by John Paul II in 1997. Confirm.
The review assumes day 43 (the sower) introduced the word 'parable'.
